title: 0/1 knapsack: subset enumeration vs meet in the middle vs pseudo-polynomial DP
problem_statement: Given n items with positive integer weights w_i and values v_i and an integer capacity W >= 0, compute the maximum total value of a subset whose total weight is at most W.

input.size_measure: Theta(n log(max value) + n log(max weight) + log W) bits. W is a number, so the input contains only log W bits for it.

algorithms.name: subset enumeration
algorithms.pseudocode: for each subset S: if w(S) <= W: best = max(best, v(S))
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(2^n n) on every input (n >= 1): exactly n 2^n inner iterations
algorithms.space_complexity: Theta(n) with the input; beyond it O(1) values (the n-bit subset mask and three running sums)

algorithms.name: meet in the middle (Horowitz-Sahni)
algorithms.idea: Split the items into halves, enumerate the 2^(n/2) subsets of each, sort one half by weight with a running maximum of value, and binary-search the best partner for every subset of the other half.
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(2^(n/2) n) in the worst case, attained whenever W >= the total weight; O(2^(n/2) n) on every input; both bounds under the machine-model assumptions in background: the built-in sort is O(m log m), bisect_right runs the documented halving loop (PROOFS.md section 2)
algorithms.correctness: Every subset is a union of a left subset and a right subset; for a fixed left subset the best right partner is the most valuable one of weight <= W - w(left), which the prefix maximum over the weight-sorted list returns (PROOFS.md section 2; credit: Horowitz & Sahni 1974).

algorithms.name: capacity DP (Bellman)
algorithms.idea: best[c] = max value achievable with capacity c, updated item by item in decreasing c so each item is used at most once.
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n W) in the worst case: exactly sum_i max(0, W - w_i + 1) inner iterations, so O(n (W + 1)) on every input and Theta(n W) whenever every w_i <= W/2; pseudo-polynomial (polynomial in the VALUE W, exponential in its bit length)
algorithms.correctness: Invariant: after t items, best[c] is the largest value of a subset of the first t items of weight <= c; the descending loop reads best[c - w] before this pass changes it, so each item is used at most once (PROOFS.md section 3).

relationship: Enumeration Theta(2^n n) -> meet in the middle Theta(2^(n/2) n) in the worst case (under the machine-model assumptions in background: the built-in sort is O(m log m), bisect_right runs the documented halving loop): an exponential-to-better-exponential improvement (T8), proved in PROOFS.md and also measured by V2 runtime fits. The DP Theta(nW) beats both whenever W << 2^(n/2), but it is NOT polynomial in the input size: adding one bit to W adds one bit to the input yet roughly doubles the DP's running time when W is much larger than the item weights (PROOFS.md section 3). That 0/1 knapsack is NP-hard, so that an algorithm polynomial in the input size would imply P = NP, is background (cited, not proved here).

verification.method: V1: all three agree on random instances (weights 1..20, values 1..30, capacity = half the total weight; enumeration up to n = 14, the others up to n = 24) and respect an independent greedy lower bound. V2: runtimes fitted against 2^n n, 2^(n/2) n and n^2 (measurements, not proofs). The DP's n^2 is specific to this harness: weights are bounded, so W = Theta(n) and Theta(nW) = Theta(n^2) (for n >= 40 the inner iterations lie between (n-2) floor(n/2) and n(10n+1); PROOFS.md section 3). The fit says nothing about large W, which is the pseudo-polynomial case. Proofs: PROOFS.md proves every claim of the entry (correctness of all three algorithms, the exact iteration counts, the time and space bounds); tests/test_proofs_knapsack.py checks the computable facts on stated ranges.

caveats: Cautionary entry (START_HERE section 4): pseudo-polynomial is not polynomial. Primary T6 rests on background: 0/1 knapsack is NP-hard, so an algorithm polynomial in the input size would imply P = NP (see background); secondary T8 for enumeration -> meet in the middle (PROOFS.md section 4; the meet-in-the-middle bound is under the machine-model assumptions in background: the built-in sort is O(m log m), bisect_right runs the documented halving loop). The DP is recorded for its teaching value, not as a pair.
notes: Good teaching case for the input-size definition in START_HERE section 1.

background.statement: 0/1 knapsack is NP-hard (its decision version is NP-complete), so an algorithm polynomial in the input size would imply P = NP; none is known.
Ibarra and Kim give fast approximation algorithms for the knapsack problem ('Fast approximation algorithms for the knapsack and sum of subset problems'); their guarantees are not restated here.
background.source: Ibarra & Kim 1975 (Journal of the ACM 22(4); title, checked against the Crossref record)

background.statement: Machine-model assumption of this entry: the built-in sort (sorted() and list.sort()) runs in O(m log m) comparisons and time in the worst case on m items. Basis, as far as the sources go: the current CPython list sort orders its merges by the powersort rule of Munro and Wild (listsort.txt), and with a plain merge powersort makes at most m H + 3m - r <= m log2 m + 3m comparisons on m items forming r runs, where H is the entropy of the run lengths (Munro & Wild 2018, Theorem 6 of the arXiv version). CPython's merges also gallop, which that theorem does not cover, so the assumption is not proved in this repository. Auger, Jugé, Nicaud and Pivoteau (2018) prove O(m log m) for the earlier TimSort merge policy of Python.
background.source: Munro & Wild 2018, Theorem 6 (arXiv version), for the plain-merge bound; Python Software Foundation, Objects/listsort.txt, for the merge order of the current CPython list sort; Auger, Jugé, Nicaud & Pivoteau 2018 (arXiv:1805.08612, abstract), for the earlier merge policy

background.statement: Machine-model assumption: on CPython, bisect_right(a, x) runs the halving loop while lo < hi: mid = (lo + hi) // 2; if x < a[mid]: hi = mid; else: lo = mid + 1, with one < comparison per iteration (the pure-Python version and the C accelerator agree), and returns the number of entries <= x of the sorted list a.
background.source: Python Software Foundation 2026, CPython source code (Lib/bisect.py, Modules/_bisectmodule.c), read 2026-10-07
